title: CORPS OF DISCOVERY
subtitle: Camp Dubois to the Pacific, 1804
introBody: Spring, 1804. Camp Dubois, Illinois. President Jefferson has charged you with leading the Corps of Discovery up the Missouri River and across the continent to the Pacific Ocean. You have a small budget, a hand-picked crew, and a mission that will change America forever. Every supply choice matters — the wilderness does not forgive poor planning.
trailFeedOpener: May 1804: The Corps of Discovery pushes off from Camp Dubois into the wide Missouri River.

events.title: The Great Falls Portage
events.text: You reach the Great Falls of the Missouri River — five massive waterfalls that block all river travel. The boats and all supplies must be carried overland for nearly 18 miles around the falls. It is backbreaking work in summer heat, and the crew is already tired.
trivia: The portage around the Great Falls took the Corps nearly a month — far longer than Lewis expected.
The men built crude wagons from cottonwood trees to haul the heavy dugout canoes overland.

sageAdvice.name: Pvt. Ordway
sageAdvice.line: If we push through fast, the men will break. A slow portage is a living portage.

sageAdvice.name: York
sageAdvice.line: I've carried heavy loads my whole life. Pace yourselves and help each other.

choices.text: Build crude wagons and take it slow — extra days but protect the crew.
choices.result: The cottonwood wagons creak and groan but hold. The portage takes 18 days. The crew arrives exhausted but intact, and spirits lift when they see open water again.

choices.text: Carry everything on backs — faster but brutal.

outcomes.result: Three men develop serious injuries from the loads. One cannot continue. The portage finishes faster, but the cost in health is steep.
The crew digs deep and carries through. Sore backs and blistered feet, but no serious injuries. Faster than the wagon method.

choices.text: Leave some supplies behind to lighten the load.
choices.result: The portage goes more quickly without the full load, but the abandoned provisions will be sorely missed in the mountains ahead.

events.title: Meeting the Shoshone
events.text: You desperately need horses to cross the Rocky Mountains, and only the Shoshone nation has them. Sacagawea, your Shoshone interpreter, recognizes the chief — he is her brother, Cameahwait. This is your best chance to obtain the horses that could make or break the expedition.
trivia: Without Shoshone horses, the Corps could not have crossed the Rocky Mountains before winter.
Sacagawea's reunion with her brother Cameahwait was one of the most emotional moments of the entire expedition.

sageAdvice.name: Sacagawea
sageAdvice.line: My people are cautious of strangers. Show respect and offer fair trade — do not rush them.

choices.text: Offer generous trade goods and let Sacagawea lead the negotiation.
choices.result: Sacagawea's presence and your generous offer of trade goods secure 29 horses and a guide. Cameahwait also shares knowledge of the mountain passes ahead. The entire camp celebrates.

choices.text: Offer minimal trade goods — save supplies for later.

outcomes.result: The Shoshone are offended by the small offer. They provide only 11 horses, barely enough, and no guide. The mountain crossing will be much harder.
Cameahwait's affection for his sister outweighs your poor offer. You receive 20 horses — not as many as possible, but enough to proceed.

choices.text: Try to take the horses by force or threat.
choices.result: A disastrous decision. The Shoshone melt into the mountains. Two crew members are wounded in the confrontation. You are left without horses and must turn back for weeks to find another route. Jefferson would not approve.

events.title: Lost in the Bitterroots
events.text: The Bitterroot Mountains are nothing like what you expected. Snow in September, no game, no trails. Your Shoshone guide Old Toby says there is a way through, but it will take everything you have. The crew is already eating tallow candles and boiled moccasins.
trivia: The Bitterroot crossing was the most brutal part of the entire journey — men went days without food in freezing mountain snow.
The Corps finally ate one of their own horses to survive the crossing.

choices.text: Trust Old Toby's knowledge — follow the Nez Perce trail exactly.

outcomes.result: Old Toby's trail is brutal but real. One man dies of exposure. The rest stagger out of the mountains onto the Camas Prairie, half-starved but alive.
Old Toby finds a shortcut through a high pass. The crossing is still terrible, but shorter than expected. The crew emerges battered but grateful.

choices.text: Send hunters ahead — risk slowing down to find food.
choices.result: Lewis and a small hunting party range ahead and shoot two deer. It is not much, but the fresh meat saves morale and keeps the weakest men on their feet through the worst of the crossing.

choices.text: Push at maximum speed — get out of the mountains before more snow falls.

outcomes.result: Two men collapse with mountain fever. One horse rolls off a cliff. The push breaks the crew's health badly, and you arrive on the far side in desperate shape.
You beat the worst snow but the pace wrecks everyone's feet and spirits. The crew survives, barely, and collapses on the western slope in relief.

events.title: The Nez Perce Nation
events.text: Starving and exhausted after the Bitterroots, your Corps stumbles onto Nez Perce land. Chief Twisted Hair greets you. The Nez Perce could easily overpower your weakened crew, but instead they offer food and show you how to build canoes from the massive ponderosa pines. Your survival depends on their goodwill.
trivia: The Nez Perce fed the starving Corps of Discovery and taught them how to hollow out canoes using fire — a technique new to the explorers.
The Nez Perce kept the Corps' horses over winter and returned them in the spring of 1806.

sageAdvice.name: Chief Twisted Hair
sageAdvice.line: We have watched your strange party struggle over the mountains. We will help you — but remember this friendship when your nation grows powerful.

choices.text: Accept their hospitality fully — rest, eat, and learn canoe-building.
choices.result: You stay four days with the Nez Perce. The crew recovers, five new canoes are built, and the sick men regain strength. Twisted Hair even draws you a map of the rivers to the ocean. This generosity may be what saves the expedition.

choices.text: Accept food but keep moving — the Pacific waits.
choices.result: You accept food gratefully but push on quickly. The Nez Perce understand urgency and wish you safe passage. You leave stronger than you arrived, though you missed the chance for new canoes.

choices.text: Trade aggressively — try to buy as much as possible.

outcomes.result: You push too hard in the trading. The Nez Perce feel their generosity is being exploited. You get the supplies but leave a sour relationship behind.
The trading goes well. Your remaining trade goods are deeply valued, and the Nez Perce send you off with more food than you could have hoped for.

events.title: Columbia River Rapids
events.text: The Columbia River races toward the Pacific through a series of violent rapids. Local Chinook people warn you that these waters have capsized many canoes. But portaging around each set of rapids would cost weeks you do not have before winter storms close the river.
events.leaveText: Portage around all rapids — safe but slow.

attempts.buttonText: Run the first set of rapids
attempts.successText: The canoes shoot through the foam and emerge intact. The crew whoops with relief. Celilo Falls roars behind you.
attempts.failureText: A canoe strikes a hidden rock. Supplies are soaked and some ammo is lost to the river.

attempts.successText: Incredible seamanship — the helmsmen thread the canoes through rocks that should have ended everything. Chinook onlookers cheer from the banks.
attempts.failureText: One canoe swamps completely. Three men nearly drown and critical supplies are lost to the Columbia.

attempts.successText: You fly through the Columbia Gorge at terrifying speed. Salt air hits your face. The ocean cannot be far. The crew is electric with excitement.
attempts.failureText: Disaster. Two canoes are destroyed in the gorge. The Corps barely makes it to shore alive. Everything must be rebuilt from scratch.

sages.name: President Thomas Jefferson
sages.title: Author of the Louisiana Purchase
sages.bio: Thomas Jefferson was the third President of the United States and the architect of the Louisiana Purchase in 1803. He commissioned the Corps of Discovery to explore the new territory, find a water route to the Pacific, and document the land, plants, animals, and peoples of the West.
sages.greeting: Before you depart, a rider arrives with a letter bearing the presidential seal. Jefferson himself has written to you with final instructions.
sages.advice: "I charge you to observe the face of the country, the soil and face of every tribe you encounter. Treat all nations with respect — you go as ambassadors of peace. The information you gather will be worth more than gold to this young nation."

question.question: Why did President Jefferson send Lewis and Clark on their expedition in 1804?
choices: To start a war with Native nations in the West
To explore the new Louisiana Territory, find a water route to the Pacific, and report on the land and people
To bring gold and silver back to Washington D.C.
To build forts along the Missouri River for the U.S. Army
question.explanation: Jefferson commissioned the Corps of Discovery after the Louisiana Purchase doubled the size of the United States. He wanted to know what the country had acquired — its geography, resources, plants, animals, and Native peoples — and to find a practical water route to the Pacific Ocean for trade.
question.teksRef: TEKS 5.1(A) — Significance of the Lewis and Clark Expedition

sages.name: Sacagawea
sages.title: Shoshone Interpreter and Guide
sages.bio: Sacagawea was a young Shoshone woman who joined the Corps of Discovery at Fort Mandan in present-day North Dakota. Traveling with her infant son Jean-Baptiste, she served as an interpreter and cultural guide, helping the Corps communicate with Native nations and signaling peaceful intentions. Her presence was invaluable to the expedition's survival.
sages.greeting: At Fort Mandan, a French-Canadian fur trader named Charbonneau approaches your camp. His young Shoshone wife, Sacagawea, steps forward and speaks clearly in her own language.
sages.advice: "I know the Shoshone lands ahead. My people have the horses you will need. I can speak for you — but you must show respect and patience. A woman traveling with a baby tells every nation you pass that this is not a war party."

question.question: How did Sacagawea help make the Lewis and Clark Expedition successful?
choices: She drew all the maps of the western United States
She served as an interpreter, helped communicate with Native peoples, and signaled that the Corps came in peace
She commanded the Corps of Discovery when Lewis was sick
She brought Spanish soldiers to protect the expedition
question.explanation: Sacagawea's most important contributions were as an interpreter and cultural ambassador. Her presence — especially traveling with an infant — reassured Native nations that the Corps was not a war party. She also helped the Corps obtain critical horses from the Shoshone, her own people, making the Rocky Mountain crossing possible.
question.teksRef: TEKS 5.1(B) — Interactions with Native peoples during the Lewis and Clark Expedition

sages.name: William Clark
sages.title: Co-Commander and Mapmaker
sages.bio: William Clark was the co-commander of the Corps of Discovery and its primary mapmaker. A skilled frontiersman and military officer, Clark drew detailed maps of the territory from his careful observations — maps that remained some of the most accurate of the American West for decades. Clark also brought York, an enslaved man, whose presence fascinated many Native nations the Corps encountered.
sages.greeting: Clark spreads a large sheet of paper across a flat boulder and invites you to look. He has been drawing maps from memory every evening, and what you see is astonishing — a detailed picture of a continent no American had ever mapped before.
sages.advice: "Every river, every mountain pass, every village — I write it all down. This information is what we were sent to gather. If we make it back, these maps will open the West to settlement. Every step you have taken has added to the knowledge of your country."

question.question: How did the Lewis and Clark Expedition contribute to westward expansion?
choices: It showed that the West was too dangerous for settlers to ever reach
It produced detailed maps and information about routes, resources, and Native peoples that encouraged future settlement
It established the first railroad route to the Pacific Ocean
It convinced the British to sell Oregon to the United States immediately
question.explanation: Clark's detailed maps and the expedition's journals gave Americans their first reliable information about the geography, resources, and peoples of the West. This knowledge directly encouraged future explorers, fur traders, and settlers to head west, fueling the westward expansion that defined 19th-century America.
question.teksRef: TEKS 5.1(A) — Role of Lewis and Clark in westward expansion

route.title: Camp Dubois
route.description: You depart from the confluence of the Missouri and Mississippi Rivers.

route.title: Missouri River Route
route.description: Steady river travel with reliable Native contacts.

route.title: Open Plains
route.description: Fast overland travel but harder resupply.

route.title: Fort Mandan
route.description: Winter quarters. Resupply with the Mandan people.

route.title: High Plains
route.description: Rich in game but exposed to weather and distance.

route.title: Rocky Mountains
route.description: The most grueling section of the entire journey.

route.title: Columbia River
route.description: Fast water to the Pacific — if the canoes hold.

route.title: Fort Clatsop — Pacific Ocean
route.description: The journey's end. The Pacific roars before you.

eventTrivia.question: Why was the Great Falls portage such a major problem for the Corps of Discovery?
choices: It was where the Corps ran out of food completely
Five waterfalls blocked the river and forced the Corps to carry everything overland for 18 miles
The Shoshone refused to let them pass the falls
eventTrivia.fact: The Great Falls of the Missouri required an 18-mile overland portage — the Corps built crude wagons from cottonwood trees to haul their heavy canoes.

eventTrivia.question: Why was Sacagawea's presence important when the Corps met new Native nations?
choices: She carried all the weapons for the Corps
A woman traveling with a baby showed Native peoples the Corps was a peaceful group, not a war party
She could run faster than any warrior and outrun danger
eventTrivia.fact: Sacagawea's presence — especially with her infant son — signaled to Native nations that the Corps of Discovery came in peace, not as a war party.

eventTrivia.question: What did the Nez Perce do for the starving Corps of Discovery after the Bitterroot Mountains?
choices: They gave the Corps guns and ammunition
They attacked the Corps to take their supplies
They fed the Corps, helped build canoes, and shared knowledge of the rivers ahead
eventTrivia.fact: The Nez Perce saved the Corps of Discovery by providing food, teaching them to build canoes, and sharing knowledge of the Columbia River system.

historicalContext: The Lewis and Clark Expedition (1804–1806) was the first American overland expedition to the Pacific coast and back. Commissioned by President Jefferson after the Louisiana Purchase, the Corps of Discovery covered nearly 8,000 miles, made first contact with dozens of Native nations, and produced the first detailed maps of the American West. The expedition's journals and maps directly fueled the westward expansion of the United States throughout the 19th century. Of the 33 permanent members, only one man died — from appendicitis — a remarkable record for the era.
